Question: Can a thunderstorm trigger allergies, or is it just the rain that causes them to flare up?
Answer: Thunderstorm can both provoke and aggravate allergies. Noise (unwanted sound) exposure may increase the risk of allergic diseases like asthma, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis. The incidence of allergic disease increases with positive night-time noise, and living in areas with high night-time noise exposure tend to have higher rates of atopic dermatitis and allergic rhinitis. [1., 2] This is presumably due to negative emotions (stress) evoked by noise that provoke sympathetic activitation of mast cells. Stresses that activate the mast cell include extreme cold, heat, noise, and light. Lightning can contribute to thunderstorm asthma (TA), also known as thunder fever, which can aggravate allergies and asthma symptoms in some people. Lightning can split bigger pollen particles in humid air into finer ones which can be easily spread by thunderstorm and get into the lungs to cause allergic symptoms such as bronchoconstriction. Lightning also forms oxides such as ozone that can damage the lungs and provoke asthmatic and allergic symptoms. Molds strive better in higher moisture seen in thunderstorm and this can provoke allergic response. 1./ 2./

Question: Why am I suffering from bronchitis and heart palpitations at the same time?
Answer: Those two conditions can be unconnected or connected. When connected, bronchitis provokes the irritation of the visceral sensory vagus nerve, which connects to the sympathetic nervous system that stimulates the heart and causes palpitations. Alternatively, bronchitis can reduce tissue oxygenation, leading to hypoxia that can lead to palpitations.

Question: What causes some people to not shiver when they have a fever?
Answer: Pyrogenic substances secreted by infectious agents and the immune system activate the hypothalamic thermostat to reset at (to) a higher level, so that heat will get to be generated up until the set temperature is attained. To achieve the rise in body temperature, aimed at increasing biochemical reactions in the immune system in a bid to get rid of the infectious agent and/or devitalized tissue, a barrage of nerve signals is sent by the hypothalamus into the skeletal muscles and the signals activate these muscles to contract and relax violently so as to to burn calories and generate heat. This is shivering thermogenesis. Some signals are sent by the hypothalamus to fat depots with the aim to enable fat cells to mobilize and burn fat from vesicles. This is non-shivering thermogenesis. If enough heat can be generated by this means, then shivering becomes redundant and certainly less likely, given how taxing and violent it is to the body. For this to be effective, the fat cells must be laden with mitochondria, and such cells constitute brown or beige fat (a hybrid of brown and white fat). Exposure to low (cold) temperatures most definitely will and exercise may promote the development of brown and beige fat. Exercise activates your body's blood hormone irisin, which tells white fat in your body to burn like brown fat. This process creates “beige fat.” When exposed to cold temperatures, stem cells called adipose progenitor cells form beige fat cells within white fat. The nervous and immune systems also help with this browning process. Brown fat can be activated by cold exposure, the sympathetic nervous system, and the thyroid hormone system. However, as people age, their response to cold temperatures weakens, which can lead to more white fat production, and this predisposes to more shivering during fever.
